result.summary: Apollo plans and founds his oracle at Delphi, then kills the she-dragon that Hera had made the nurse of Typhaon. The text tells how Hera, angered by Zeus over Athena's birth, bore Typhaon alone. Apollo also buries the spring of Telphusa, who had deceived him.

scenes.title: Apollo founds his temple
scenes.summary: Apollo announces his oracle and lays out the foundations. Trophonius and Agamedes lay the stone footing, and men build the temple.

scenes.title: The dragoness and Typhaon
scenes.summary: Apollo kills the she-dragon by the spring. The narrator recalls she raised Typhaon, born of Hera's anger at Zeus.
scenes.stakes: The dragoness faces death; men suffer her mischief.

scenes.title: Hera's complaint to the gods
scenes.summary: Hera complains before the gods that Zeus bore Athena alone. She threatens to bear a mightier son and withdraws from Zeus.
scenes.stakes: Hera's honour as wife; Zeus risks being rivalled by a stronger son.

scenes.title: Hera prays and bears Typhaon
scenes.summary: Hera strikes the earth and calls on the Titans. After a year she bears Typhaon and gives him to the dragoness.
scenes.stakes: Mankind will suffer the monster's plague.

scenes.title: Apollo slays the dragoness
scenes.summary: Apollo shoots the dragoness, who dies in agony. He boasts over her, and the place is named Pytho because she rotted there.

scenes.title: Apollo buries Telphusa's spring
scenes.summary: Apollo, angry at Telphusa's deception, buries her stream under rocks and builds an altar there, earning the name Telphusian.
scenes.stakes: Telphusa loses her stream and sole renown.

alias_notes.explanation: Apollo's epithet, explained as from Pytho, where the monster rotted.
Epithet from his humbling of the stream Telphusa.
Variant name of the same monster.

notable_quotes.reason: Apollo's boast over the dying dragoness, source of the Pytho etymology.

analysis.text: The hymn presents Apollo's oracle as won by violence, replacing older earth powers such as the dragoness and Telphusa.
The passage gives a folk etymology of Pytho and Pythian from the Greek verb meaning to rot, explaining Delphi's cult names.

legacy.text: The myth of Apollo slaying the Python became a standard subject of Greek and later European art and literature, and gave the name Pythian Games.

fun_facts.text: Trophonius and Agamedes were later said to be legendary architects, and Trophonius had his own oracle at Lebadea.

language_notes.text: A hecatomb was originally a sacrifice of a hundred oxen; here it means a grand public sacrifice. "Perfect" means unblemished.
Peloponnesus is the large southern peninsula of mainland Greece; "Europe" here likely means the mainland north of it.
"Wont" means accustomed; "thin-shanked" describes the sheep's slender legs.
"Bare" is the old past tense of "bear"; "in his head" refers to Athena's birth from Zeus's head.
"Shrivelled of foot" means lame or deformed in the feet; Hephaestus was traditionally lame.
The question means: should I not have borne you a child, since I at least was called your wife?
Striking the ground with the hand was a gesture used to call on the powers below, here the Titans, to hear her prayer.
"No wit lesser" means not at all lesser; Hera asks for a son stronger than Zeus, just as Zeus is stronger than his father Cronos.
"Bare" is an old past tense of "bear"; "fell" here means fierce or deadly.
"Day of doom" means the day of death; the sentence says anyone who met the dragoness was destroyed.
A hecatomb was a large sacrifice, originally of a hundred oxen; "perfect" means unblemished.
Typhoeus and Chimera are monsters; Typhoeus is a fearsome son of Earth, and the Chimera is a fire-breathing hybrid beast. Apollo says even they could not save her.
The name Pytho is explained by the Greek verb pythein, "to rot". Apollo's title Pythian is derived from the place.

context_notes.text: Trophonius and Agamedes were legendary master builders, said in tradition to have built Apollo's temple at Delphi.
Typhaon is a monstrous being, here raised by the dragoness; he is a separate figure from Typhoeus in some tales.
Thetis, a sea goddess, later became the mother of Achilles.
The Titans are the older generation of gods, defeated by Zeus and imprisoned in Tartarus, the deep underworld pit.
Helios is the Sun god; his heat is said to rot the corpse. Hyperion is a Titan associated with the sun.
Apollo's cult title Telphusian links him to the spring Telphusa, near which he had an altar.

literary_notes.text: "Bloated, great she-dragon" and "bloody plague" characterize the monster as loathsome, justifying her death.
"Cloud-gathering" is Zeus's stock epithet, here used ironically as Hera complains of him.
Hera turns from the assembly to address Zeus directly, though he is not present, which heightens her indignation.
Hera's threat to leave his bed shows her proud, vengeful nature and her insistence on marital honor.
Striking the earth is a ritual act that adds force to her curse and calls the underworld powers to listen.
"One evil thing to another such" pairs the monstrous child with the dragoness, stressing how evil is joined to evil.
Sound and bloody breath make the dragoness's death vivid and horrifying.
Apollo's taunt "rot here" turns into the place's name, so his insult becomes a permanent title.
